content: This one is near and dear to me (as I've spent many summers thinking about this problem). Apparently, it was recently resolved negatively: https://github.com/tadamcz/koethe/tree/main

@Tom Adamczewski did you (or one of your collaborators) edit the wikipedia article on this problem, or was this user someone else who caught wind of your announcement?

I'm asking because the edit mentions your name twice, and includes signs of AI writing such as broken LaTeX and lines like:

The Lean kernel verified the proof, which consists of over 3,300 lines of code with zero sorry stubs or unverified axioms.
I definitely did not edit Wikipedia! That's cringe
If you're a Wikipedia contributor, can you revert the edit?
Yes, I'll change it now. Just wanted to check before accidentally getting your wikipedia account banned lol

Two ring theorists have written to me and are going to write up the result properly. Once that is out, eventually Wikipedia editors might update the page, but they should do that at their own pace. I'm not in a rush here.

It's up on the arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07996

We construct a counterexample to Köthe's conjecture and use this to also answer a question due to Rowen.

I do not understand the paper at all -- what a strange world we live in! I insisted on a contribution statement that explains I only did the AI bits.
That abstract is odd, since they didn't construct the counterexample, but rather slightly modified a counterexample created by an LLM.
There is a contribution statement at the end that explains the role of AI in various stages of the paper.
What do you think the abstract should say?

Putting a contribution statement at the end of a paper doesn't cut it. Whenever someone uses an idea from someone else (including a machine) they should give it credit at the point it is used (including in the abstract if it is a major part, and during the construction). Otherwise it creates a false impression.

There are a couple other things that trouble me about this preprint, including things in the contribution statement, but for the authors' sake I don't want to get into it publicly. We are in a new world, so I don't want to be too harsh about navigating these issues!

By the way, this was the third write-up of the example I've seen; an earlier one is available at MO, and another was created by a colleague of mine (asking Claude to write it). All this was done before this arXiv write-up! We are indeed in "a strange world".
Please feel free to write to us privately if you prefer. Emails in the paper.
I’m not a mathematician, I don’t have a dog in this fight. I personally would be happy to make any reasonable adjustments to the paper.

Of course you (or anyone) should feel free to write a different or better exposition of the AI proof, or to build on it in a different way.

I just want to help the maths community, while doing my job, which is to study the capabilities of AI systems scientifically.

Tom Adamczewski said:

I’m not a mathematician, I don’t have a dog in this fight. I personally would be happy to make any reasonable adjustments to the paper.

Now that the paper is on the arXiv, things will slow down a bit. Feedback from others will come naturally. It is definitely standard practice to submit revisions to the arXiv, so you don't need to worry.

My main comment (for your coauthors) is simply: be extremely clear what ideas were, and were not, contributed by the LLMs. Cite those contributions at the time they are used, and in the abstract if they form a major part of the construction. Don't overstate one's own involvement, or include in "we" a non-coauthor like Chat.

And by the way, I should say that I very much appreciate how open you have been about all this, including posting the lean code. Great job!

Concerning attributing AI, here is an example from my colleagues: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15850

The end of the abstract is:
"...The proofs in this paper are due to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Pro, and the paper is merely an exposition of its output. The proofs has been verified by the authors and they take full responsibility for any errors."
